# Chapter 19: Empirical Processes

[Worked problems for Chapter 19](problems.qmd#problems-chapter-19)

- take the ordinary law of large numbers and central limit theorem and make them **uniform over classes of functions**.
- The central object is the empirical measure $\mathbb P_n$ and the empirical process $\mathbb G_n$.
- The main conceptual distinction is:
    - **Glivenko–Cantelli class** = uniform law of large numbers.
    - **Donsker class** = uniform central limit theorem.
- Donsker conditions let us control empirical processes evaluated at **estimated/random functions**, such as functions involving estimated nuisance parameters.

## 19.1 Empirical Distribution Functions

- For i.i.d. observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with distribution function $F$, define the empirical distribution function $\mathbb F_n(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n1\{X_i\leq t\}$.
- For each fixed $t$, the ordinary law of large numbers gives $\mathbb F_n(t)\overset {a.s.} \to F(t)$.
- For each fixed $t$, the ordinary central limit theorem gives $\sqrt n(\mathbb F_n(t)-F(t))\rightsquigarrow N(0,F(t)(1-F(t)))$.
- Chapter 19 asks for stronger results that hold **simultaneously over all** $t$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic:**

$$
\sqrt n\,\|\mathbb F_n-F\|_\infty=\sup_t\left|\sqrt n\bigl(\mathbb F_n(t)-F(t)\bigr)\right|.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 19.1: Glivenko–Cantelli

- The empirical CDF converges uniformly to the true CDF: $|\mathbb F_n-F|_\infty=\underset t \sup|\mathbb F_n(t)-F(t)|\overset{a.s.}\longrightarrow0$.
- This is a **uniform law of large numbers**.
- Compare:
    - pointwise LLN: $\mathbb F_n(t)\to F(t)$ for each fixed $t$;
    - Glivenko–Cantelli: $\sup_t|\mathbb F_n(t)-F(t)|\to0$.
:::

### Proof idea

- Partition the real line into finitely many intervals on which $F$ changes by at most $\varepsilon$.
- Use pointwise convergence at the finitely many endpoints.
- Monotonicity of $F_n$ and $F$ controls all points between the endpoints.
- The main idea is **finite approximation + control between approximation points**, echoing Chapter 18.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 19.3: Donsker

- The process $\sqrt n(\mathbb F_n-F)$ converges as a random function to an $F$-Brownian bridge $\mathbb G_F$.
- The limit is a zero-mean Gaussian process with covariance $E[\mathbb G_F(s)\mathbb G_F(t)]=F(s\wedge t)-F(s)F(t)$.
- Thus Donsker is the **functional/uniform analogue of the central limit theorem**.
- the abstract empirical-process theory in §19.2 explains when such results hold.
:::

$$
\text{Glivenko--Cantelli}=\text{uniform LLN}
$$

$$
\text{Donsker}=\text{uniform CLT}
$$

- The rest of the chapter generalizes these two ideas from the class of indicator functions $1_{\{x\leq t\}}$ to arbitrary classes of functions.

## 19.2 Empirical Distributions

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Empirical measure notation

- Let $P$ be the distribution of $X_1,\ldots,X_n$.
- The empirical distribution is $\mathbb P_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$.
- For a measurable function $f$, write $\mathbb P_nf=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nf(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f,dP$.
- Thus $\mathbb P_nf$ is simply the sample average of $f(X)$.

### Empirical process notation

- Define the empirical process by $\mathbb G_nf=\sqrt n(\mathbb P_n-P)f=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n{f(X_i)-Pf}$.
- For one fixed $f$ with $Pf^2<\infty$, the ordinary CLT gives $\mathbb G_nf\rightsquigarrow N(0,Pf^2-(Pf)^2)$.
- The empirical-process question is what happens **uniformly over** $f\in\mathcal F$.
- We therefore treat $f\mapsto\mathbb G_nf$ as one random function in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Glivenko–Cantelli classes

- A class $\mathcal F$ is called $P$Glivenko–Cantelli if $|\mathbb P_n-P|*{\mathcal F}=\sup*{f\in\mathcal F}|\mathbb P_nf-Pf|\overset{a.s.*}\longrightarrow0$.
- This says the LLN holds **uniformly over the whole class** $\mathcal F$.
:::

- A finite class of integrable functions is automatically Glivenko–Cantelli.
- If $\mathcal F$ is extremely large, pointwise LLNs need not combine into a uniform LLN.
- Thus we need ways to measure the **size/complexity** of $\mathcal F$.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Donsker classes

- A class $\mathcal F$ is called $P$Donsker if the process ${\mathbb G_nf:f\in\mathcal F}$ converges weakly in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ to a tight Gaussian process $\mathbb G_P$.
- The limiting process has mean zero and covariance $E[\mathbb G_Pf,\mathbb G_Pg]=Pfg-PfPg$.
- This Gaussian limit is called a $P$**Brownian bridge**.
:::

- For every finite set $f_1,\ldots,f_k$, the ordinary multivariate CLT already gives convergence of ${\mathbb G_nf_1,\ldots,\mathbb G_nf_k}$.
- The Donsker property adds enough uniform control to obtain convergence of the **entire process**.

$$
\text{finite-dimensional CLT}+\text{asymptotic equicontinuity}\Rightarrow\text{Donsker convergence}
$$

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Envelope function

- An envelope for $\mathcal F$ is a function $F$ such that $|f(x)|\leq F(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and every $x$.
- Moment conditions on the envelope control how large functions in the class can be.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Brackets

- Given functions $l$ and $u$ with $l\leq u$, the bracket $[l,u]$ consists of all functions $f$ satisfying $l\leq f\leq u$.
- An $\varepsilon$-bracket in $L_r(P)$ satisfies $|u-l|*{P,r}<\varepsilon$, where $|f|*{P,r}=(P|f|^r)^{1/r}$.
- The **bracketing number** $N_{[]}(\varepsilon,\mathcal F,L_r(P))$ is the minimum number of $\varepsilon$brackets needed to cover $\mathcal F$.
- The smaller the bracketing number, the smaller the effective complexity of $\mathcal F$.
:::

- Replace the possibly infinite class $\mathcal F$ with finitely many approximating brackets.
- If sufficiently few brackets are needed at increasingly fine scales, the empirical process can be uniformly controlled.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 19.4: Glivenko–Cantelli via bracketing

- If $N_{[]}(\varepsilon,\mathcal F,L_1(P))<\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, then $\mathcal F$ is $P$Glivenko–Cantelli.
- At every desired level of accuracy, $\mathcal F$ can be approximated by finitely many functions.
- The ordinary LLN can therefore be made uniform.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 19.5: Donsker via bracketing entropy

- Define the bracketing entropy integral $J_{[]}(\delta,\mathcal F,L_2(P))=\int_0^\delta\sqrt{\log N_{[]}(\varepsilon,\mathcal F,L_2(P))},d\varepsilon$.
- If $J_{[]}(1,\mathcal F,L_2(P))<\infty$, then $\mathcal F$ is $P$Donsker.
:::

- For a uniform CLT, finite approximation at every scale is not enough.
- The complexity of the class cannot increase **too quickly** as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
- The entropy integral measures the accumulated complexity over increasingly fine approximation scales.

### Proof idea

1. Finite-dimensional convergence follows from the ordinary multivariate CLT.
2. Use bracketing and maximal inequalities to control $\sup_{f,g\text{ close}}|\mathbb G_n(f-g)|$.
3. This establishes asymptotic equicontinuity.
4. Apply Theorem 18.14.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{\text{entropy condition}\Rightarrow\text{equicontinuity}\Rightarrow\text{Donsker}}
$$

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 19.6: Distribution functions

- Take $\mathcal F={1_{(-\infty,t]}:t\in\mathbb R}$.
- Brackets can be constructed by dividing the distribution into intervals containing little probability mass.
- The entropy condition easily holds.
- Therefore the classical Donsker theorem is a special case of the abstract theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 19.7: Parametric classes

- Suppose $\mathcal F={f_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d}$ and $|f_{\theta_1}(x)-f_{\theta_2}(x)|\leq m(x)|\theta_1-\theta_2|$.
- If $Pm^2<\infty$ and $\Theta$ is bounded, the class has polynomially growing bracketing numbers and is Donsker.
- Main lesson: **ordinary finite-dimensional smooth parametric families are typically Donsker under mild moment conditions**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
### Examples 19.9–19.10: Smooth function classes

- Sufficiently smooth infinite-dimensional classes also have controlled entropy.
- Main takeaway only:
    - more smoothness makes the class effectively smaller;
    - sufficiently smooth classes are Donsker.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 19.11: Bounded variation

- Classes of monotone functions, and more generally functions of bounded variation, are Donsker under broad conditions.
- Chapter 25 uses bounded-variation arguments when verifying Donsker conditions.
:::

### VC classes

- VC classes provide another convenient way of showing that a class is not too large.
- A class has finite VC dimension if it cannot represent arbitrarily complicated patterns on finite sets.
- Finite VC dimension implies polynomial covering-number growth.
- With suitable envelope moment conditions, this gives Glivenko–Cantelli and Donsker properties.

$$
\boxed{\text{VC class}\Rightarrow\text{polynomial entropy}\Rightarrow\text{GC/Donsker}}
$$

::: {.callout-tip title="Example"}
### Example 19.20: Stability under Lipschitz transformations

- Donsker classes remain Donsker under many simple transformations.
- In particular, if $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$ are Donsker with suitable envelopes, then classes formed by sums, minima, maxima, and under boundedness conditions products can also be Donsker.
- This is useful because complicated estimating functions can often be constructed from simpler known Donsker classes.
:::

## 19.4 Random Functions

- So far, Donsker theory controls $\mathbb G_nf$ uniformly for deterministic $f\in\mathcal F$.
- In statistics we often evaluate the empirical process at an **estimated function** $\widehat f_n$.
- For example, $\widehat f_n=f_{\widehat\theta_n}$.
- Because $\widehat f_n$ depends on the same observations that define $\mathbb G_n$, we cannot simply apply an ordinary CLT conditional on $\widehat f_n$.
- Donsker theory solves this through **stochastic equicontinuity**.

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 19.24

Suppose:

- $\mathcal F$ is $P$Donsker;
- $\widehat f_n\in\mathcal F$;
- $P(\widehat f_n-f_0)^2\overset P\longrightarrow0$.

Then:

$$
\boxed{\mathbb G_n(\widehat f_n-f_0)\overset P\longrightarrow0}
$$

and consequently:

$$
\boxed{\mathbb G_n\widehat f_n=\mathbb G_nf_0+o_P(1).}
$$

:::

- If $\widehat f_n$ is close to $f_0$ in $L_2(P)$, then they are close according to the natural variance semimetric of the limiting Gaussian process.
- Because $\mathcal F$ is Donsker, the limiting Brownian bridge has uniformly continuous sample paths in this semimetric.
- Therefore the empirical process cannot asymptotically distinguish $\widehat f_n$ from $f_0$.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{L_2(P)\text{ closeness of functions}+\text{Donsker equicontinuity}\Rightarrow\text{empirical-process closeness}.}
$$

**Proof.**

- Define $g(z,f)=z(f)-z(f_0)$.
- Because $\mathcal F$ is Donsker, $\mathbb G_n\rightsquigarrow\mathbb G_P$ in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$.
- Because $P(\widehat f_n-f_0)^2\overset P\to0$, we have $\widehat f_n\overset P\to f_0$ in the $L_2(P)$ semimetric.
- Therefore $(\mathbb G_n,\widehat f_n)\rightsquigarrow(\mathbb G_P,f_0)$.
- By Lemma 18.15, almost every sample path $f\mapsto\mathbb G_Pf$ is continuous under the relevant semimetric.
- Hence $g$ is continuous at $(\mathbb G_P,f_0)$ almost surely.
- Apply the continuous mapping theorem: $\mathbb G_n(\widehat f_n-f_0)\rightsquigarrow\mathbb G_P(f_0)-\mathbb G_P(f_0)=0$.
- Because the limit is constant, convergence in distribution to zero is equivalent to convergence in probability.

This proof is essentially:

$$
\boxed{\text{Donsker convergence}+\text{Lemma 18.15}+\text{continuous mapping}.}
$$

- In semiparametric models, efficient scores and influence functions typically involve unknown nuisance parameters.
- In practice we replace them with estimated versions.
- Lemma 19.24 gives conditions under which $\mathbb G_n\widetilde\ell_{\widehat\eta_n}=\mathbb G_n\widetilde\ell_{\eta_0}+o_P(1)$.
- Once this replacement is justified, an ordinary CLT can often finish the argument.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 19.26: Infinite-dimensional Z-estimation

- A Z-estimator solves estimating equations.
- In a finite-dimensional model we might solve $\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}=0$.
- In semiparametric models, the parameter may be infinite-dimensional and we may have an entire collection of estimating equations indexed by $h\in H$.
- Van der Vaart explicitly introduces Theorem 19.26 as useful for the treatment of semiparametric models in Chapter 25.

### Setup

- Let $\psi_{\theta,h}$ be estimating functions indexed by a parameter $\theta$ and $h\in H$.
- Think of $P\psi_\theta$ as a function of $h$, hence an element of $\ell^\infty(H)$.
- Suppose $\theta_0$ solves the population equations $P\psi_{\theta_0}=0$.
- The estimator approximately solves $|\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}|_H=o_P(n^{-1/2})$.

Under Donsker, consistency, and differentiability conditions,

$$
V\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)=-\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1).
$$

- Here $V$ is the derivative of the population map $\theta\mapsto P\psi_\theta$.

This is the infinite-dimensional analogue of the familiar Z-estimator expansion.

The basic decomposition is:

$$
0\approx\sqrt n\,\mathbb P_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}=\mathbb G_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}+\sqrt n\,P\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}.
$$

Then:

- Donsker stochastic equicontinuity gives $\mathbb G_n\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}=\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1)$;
- differentiability gives $\sqrt n\,P\psi_{\widehat\theta_n}=V\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)+o_P(1)$.

Therefore:

$$
V\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)=-\mathbb G_n\psi_{\theta_0}+o_P(1).
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{empirical-process linearization}+\text{population linearization}\Rightarrow\text{asymptotic linearity of the estimator}.}
$$

:::

## 19.5 Changing Classes

- Previous results assume a fixed class $\mathcal F$ for every $n$.
- Sometimes the relevant class itself changes with the sample size, giving $\mathcal F_n$.
- This arises, for example, after local rescaling around an estimated parameter.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 19.28

- Extends Donsker-type weak convergence to classes $\mathcal F_n$ that change with $n$.
- The same basic ingredients remain:
    - finite-dimensional Gaussian convergence;
    - control of the size of the changing classes through entropy;
    - asymptotic equicontinuity.
:::

## 19.6 Maximal Inequalities

- To prove asymptotic equicontinuity, we need to control quantities such as $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\mathbb G_nf|$.
- A **maximal inequality** gives a probabilistic or expectation bound on such a supremum.
- These inequalities provide the technical bridge from **entropy of a function class** to **uniform control of its empirical process**.

$$
\boxed{\text{Bernstein inequality}\rightarrow\text{finite maxima}\rightarrow\text{chaining}\rightarrow\text{maximal inequality}.}
$$

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 19.34

- This is the main maximal inequality underlying the bracketing Donsker theorem.
- Conceptually, it says that if:
    - every function in $\mathcal F$ is small in $L_2(P)$;
    - the class has small bracketing entropy;
    - the envelope is controlled;
- then $E^*|\mathbb G_n|_{\mathcal F}$ is small.
:::

$$
\boxed{\text{small functions}+\text{small class}\Rightarrow\text{small empirical-process supremum}.}
$$

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 19.36

- Applies to uniformly bounded classes with $Pf^2<\delta^2$ and $|f|_\infty\leq M$.
- It bounds $E^*|\mathbb G_n|_{\mathcal F}$ in terms of the bracketing entropy integral and the size parameters $\delta$ and $M$.
- Interpretation: entropy plus local $L_2$ size yields a quantitative stochastic bound.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 19.37

- Gives an analogous bound using a stronger Bernstein-type norm.
- Again, its role is to convert complexity bounds into control of the empirical process.
:::

Summary

$$
\boxed{\mathbb P_n-P\rightarrow\mathbb G_n=\sqrt n(\mathbb P_n-P)}
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{GC}=\text{uniform LLN},\qquad\text{Donsker}=\text{uniform CLT}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{entropy/bracketing/VC conditions}\rightarrow\text{Donsker property}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{Donsker}+\widehat f_n\to f_0\text{ in }L_2(P)\rightarrow\mathbb G_n(\widehat f_n-f_0)=o_P(1)}
$$

and therefore, for estimation,

$$
\boxed{\text{estimated nuisance function}\rightarrow\text{replace by true nuisance function at first order}.}
$$
